query: For high-entropy nanoalloys in high-temperature applications, what governs structural and chemical stability, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, propose a controlled comparison that would distinguish it from alternatives, predict observations relative to a baseline, define the boundaries of the prediction, identify supporting evidence from the background, and state a falsifying outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy nanoalloys used for high‐temperature applications, the combination of high configurational entropy and nanoscale grain boundary/interfacial energy barriers is the dominant factor that preserves both structural and chemical homogeneity. In these materials, the random atomic distribution (high entropy) suppresses phase segregation at moderate temperatures, while the high energy of nanosized grain boundaries (or interactions with a passivating support) acts to arrest coarsening and chemical separation. However, once thermal energy exceeds a critical threshold, atomic mobility increases sufficiently to overcome these stabilizing effects, leading to observable clustering or phase separation.
generation.material_initial_state: Uniform high-entropy nanoalloys (e.g., sub-10 nm particles or thin films) with random elemental occupancy and well-defined nanoscale grain boundaries, as synthesized via rapid reduction (e.g., laser-induced thermionic emission reduction) leading to inherent support-mediated stabilization.
generation.intervention: Controlled heat treatment at varying temperatures (including temperatures both below and above the predicted critical thermal threshold) under an inert atmosphere.
generation.conditions: Samples are heated with a well-defined temperature ramp in an inert environment, comparing treatments at a moderate temperature (e.g., 800 °C) versus a high temperature (e.g., 1100 °C). Grain size and support interface quality must be kept consistent between samples.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale grain boundaries and the interfacial interactions with the defective carbon (or similar) support in synthesis, which together provide energy barriers that slow atomic diffusion and prevent premature phase segregation.
generation.mechanism: The high configurational entropy of multi-element systems statistically stabilizes the solid solution, opposing chemical segregation. At the nanoscale, grain boundaries and support interfaces add an extra barrier to atomic rearrangements. As temperature increases, the enhanced atomic mobility eventually overcomes these barriers, leading to clustering and phase separation. This competition sets a threshold temperature below which the structure remains stable.
generation.predicted_outcome: Below the critical temperature, high-entropy nanoalloys will retain a single-phase, homogeneous structure with minimal elemental segregation. Above this temperature threshold, increased atomic diffusion will lead to detectable clustering or phase segregation (e.g., formation of secondary phases or inhomogeneous elemental distributions) relative to the baseline.
generation.baseline: Nanoalloy samples maintained at a moderate treatment temperature (e.g., 800 °C) that show a uniform single-phase microstructure with consistent elemental distribution.
generation.boundary: The prediction is expected to hold for nanoalloys with grain sizes in the nanometer regime (below ~10 nm) and for high-temperature exposures up to around 1100 °C. Beyond these conditions (e.g., much larger grains or in cases where the support interactions differ significantly), additional mechanisms might dominate the stability behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The exact threshold temperature and the quantitative contribution of the nanoscale grain boundary energy are uncertain and may vary among different high-entropy alloy systems and synthesis routes. Further calibration with experimental data is required.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a controlled set of high-entropy nanoalloy samples with identical composition and initial microstructure. Divide them into two groups: one group is subjected to heat treatment at a moderate temperature (e.g., 800 °C) and the other group at a higher temperature (e.g., 1100 °C). Ensure that environmental variables such as atmosphere and heating rate are consistent. After treatment, use high-resolution TEM, XRD, and EDS mapping to compare the phase homogeneity and elemental distributions between the two groups.
measurements: Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) for grain size and phase contrast
Energy-Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (EDS) for mapping elemental homogeneity
X-Ray Diffraction (XRD) for phase identification and detection of secondary phases
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If nanoalloy samples treated at the high temperature (e.g., 1100 °C) do not display statistically significant increases in atomic clustering, phase segregation, or the emergence of secondary phases compared to the moderate temperature (800 °C) baseline, then the hypothesis that nanoscale grain boundaries and configurational entropy are the primary stabilizing factors is falsified.

(Mg,Mn,Fe,Co,Ni)O: A rocksalt high-entropy oxide containing divalent Mn and Fe

Abstract: High-entropy oxides (HEOs) have aroused growing interest due to fundamental questions relating to their structure formation, phase stability, and the interplay between configurational disorder and physical and chemical properties. Introducing Fe(II) and Mn(II) into a rocksalt HEO is considered challenging, as theoretical analysis suggests that they are unstable in this structure under ambient conditions. Here, we develop a bottom-up method for synthesizing Mn- and Fe-containing rocksalt HEO (FeO-HEO). We present a comprehensive investigation of its crystal structure and the random cation-site occupancy. We show the improved structural robustness of this FeO-HEO and verify the viability of an oxygen sublattice as a buffer layer. Compositional analysis reveals the valence and spin state of the iron species. We further report the antiferromagnetic order of this FeO-HEO below the transition temperature ~218 K and predict the conditions of phase stability of Mn- and Fe-containing HEOs. Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties

Nanoalloy libraries from laser-induced thermionic emission reduction

Abstract: Nanoalloys, especially high-entropy nanoalloys (HENAs) that contain equal stoichiometric metallic elements in each nanoparticle, are widely used in vast applications. Currently, the synthesis of HENAs is challenged by slow reaction kinetics that leads to phase segregation, sophisticated pretreatment of precursors, and inert conditions that preclude scalable fabrication of HENAs. Here, we report direct conversion of metal salts to ultrafine HENAs on carbonaceous support by nanosecond pulsed laser under atmospheric conditions. Because of the unique laser-induced thermionic emission and etch on carbon, the reduced metal elements were gathered to ultrafine HENAs and stabilized by defective carbon support. This scalable, facile, and low-cost method overcomes the immiscible issue and can produce various HENAs uniformly with a size of 1 to 3 nanometers and metal elements up to 11 with productivity up to 7 grams per hour.
